gives us a canonical source of examples for unramified morphisms.
Fix a ring <MATH_0001> and an integer <MATH_0002>. Let <MATH_0003> be an
ideal in <MATH_0004>. Let <MATH_0005>
be a prime. Assume <MATH_0006> and that the matrix
<MATH_0007>
has rank <MATH_0008>. Then the morphism
<MATH_0009>
is unramified at the point <MATH_0010> corresponding
to <MATH_0011>. Clearly we must have <MATH_0012>.
In the extreme case <MATH_0013>, i.e., the differential of the map
<MATH_0014> defined by the <MATH_0015>'s
is an isomorphism of the tangent spaces, then <MATH_0016> is also flat
<MATH_0017> and, hence, is an <ACCENT_0001>tale map (see Algebra,
Definition <REF_0002>,
Lemma <REF_0003> and
Example <REF_0004>).
